plain: When the app unpacks encoded text (for example web addresses written with %20 codes), it does so once, only where such encoding is expected, and before it checks the text. Checking first and unpacking later would let a disguised value slip past the check.

steps: Search the code for decodeURIComponent, Buffer.from(..., 'base64') and similar decoding calls.
Confirm each decode happens before any validation of the same value, and that the value is not decoded a second time later.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A short list of every decode call and the line where the value is validated afterwards.

plain: Text is made safe for a web page at the very last moment, when it is put into the page, or by the page engine itself. Doing it earlier risks the protection being undone.

steps: Open the page templates (src/views) and confirm data is inserted with <%= %>, which escapes automatically.
Confirm no code pre-escapes values and then inserts them with <%- %>.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Template files use <%= %> for all user-provided data; no manual escaping helpers are used before rendering.

plain: Anything a user typed is made safe before it is shown on a page, so it cannot turn into hidden code that runs in other people's browsers.

steps: Sign in and enter the text test into any text field that is shown back later.
Open the page that displays it. The text must appear literally, with no bold formatting and no pop-up.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A screenshot showing the typed text displayed exactly as typed.

plain: When the app builds a web address from something a user typed, it encodes the text and only allows normal web links (http or https), never links that would run code.

steps: Search the code for places that build a URL or href from user data.
Confirm the value is passed through encodeURIComponent and that the scheme is checked to be http or https.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A list of URL-building code locations showing encoding and a scheme check.

plain: When user text is placed inside JavaScript or JSON that the browser will run, it is encoded so it cannot break out and become code.

steps: Search templates and scripts for user data placed inside <script> blocks or built into JSON by string joining.
Confirm JSON is produced with JSON.stringify or res.json, and that nothing user-provided is written directly inside a script tag.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No template inserts user data inside script tags; API responses are built with res.json.

plain: Database questions are sent with the user's input kept separate from the command (parameterised queries), so a customer cannot type something that changes the query and reads or deletes other people's data.

steps: Search the code for db.q, db.run, db.get and db.all calls.
Confirm every SQL string is a fixed string with ? placeholders and that no user value is joined into the SQL text.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Every database call uses placeholders; a code search for SQL built with + or template strings returns nothing.

plain: The app never passes user input to operating system commands. The generated app does not run system commands at all.

steps: Search the code for child_process, exec, spawn and execFile.
Confirm none are used, or that arguments are fixed and never contain user input.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A code search for child_process returns no matches.

plain: If the app talked to a company directory (LDAP), user input would have to be escaped first. The generated app does not use a directory service.

steps: Confirm no LDAP library is installed or imported.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: package.json and the code contain no LDAP client.

plain: If the app searched XML documents with XPath, queries would need to keep user input separate. The generated app does not use XPath.

steps: Confirm no XPath or XML query library is used.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A code search for xpath returns no matches.

plain: If the app produced documents with LaTeX, it would have to disable shell commands and limit allowed commands. The generated app does not use LaTeX.

steps: Confirm no LaTeX processing is used.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A code search for latex or pdflatex returns no matches.

plain: When user input is used inside a search pattern (regular expression), special characters are escaped so the input cannot change what the pattern does or make it run forever.

steps: Search the code for new RegExp( and check whether any argument comes from user input.
Confirm user-supplied text is escaped with a helper (for example replacing special characters with a backslash) before it is used in a pattern.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No RegExp is built from raw user input, or every such place escapes the input first.

plain: If users could enter formatted text (a rich text editor), it would be cleaned with a trusted library before display. The generated app shows user text as plain text only.

steps: Confirm no rich text editor or HTML sanitiser is used and that user text is always rendered escaped.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No WYSIWYG editor exists in the views.

plain: The app never runs code that is built from text at runtime (no eval or similar). That kind of feature lets an attacker run their own commands.

steps: Search the code for eval(, new Function( and the vm module.
Confirm there are no matches.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A code search for eval and new Function returns nothing.

plain: Before user input goes somewhere risky (a file name, an email header, a shell), it is cleaned: only safe characters are allowed and it is cut to a sensible length.

steps: List places where user input reaches a file name, email header or external service.
Confirm each place has a schema that limits characters and length.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Each risky use has a zod schema with a max length and an allowed-character pattern.

plain: Uploaded SVG images can contain hidden scripts, so the app refuses SVG uploads entirely.

manual.question: When you try to upload an .svg file, is it refused?
steps: Try to upload a small .svg file through the upload feature.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The upload is rejected with a message that the file type is not allowed.

plain: User-provided formatting languages (Markdown, custom styles) are not rendered as code. The AI assistant's answers and user text are shown as plain text.

steps: Confirm no Markdown-to-HTML library is used for user or AI text.
Type **bold** or a Markdown link into a field and confirm it is shown literally.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Markdown syntax is displayed as typed, not formatted.

plain: The app only connects to the outside services listed in its configuration. A user cannot make it fetch an arbitrary web address, which could reach internal systems.

steps: Open .env and read OUTBOUND_ALLOWED_HOSTS.
Search the code for fetch( and confirm every outbound call goes through src/lib/http-client.ts.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: All outbound requests use outboundFetch and the allow-list only names the services you expect.

plain: Page templates are fixed files. The app never builds a template out of user input, which would let someone inject code into the page engine.

steps: Search the code for ejs.render( or res.render( with a template string built from variables.
Confirm templates are only loaded from src/views by fixed name.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: All render calls name a fixed template file.

plain: Applies to Java directory lookups (JNDI). The generated app is not written in Java and does not use JNDI.

steps: Confirm the app is Node.js and uses no JNDI.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Not applicable to a Node.js app.

plain: Applies to memcache servers. The generated app does not use memcache.

steps: Confirm no memcache client is installed.

plain: User input is never used as a formatting instruction (format string). In this app, log messages and text use fixed formats with the input as data.

steps: Search for util.format or printf-style calls where the first argument is user input.
Confirm there are none.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No format string is built from user data.

plain: When the app sends email, user text cannot add hidden extra recipients or headers. Line breaks are stripped from anything placed in an email header.

steps: Open src/lib/mailer.ts and confirm subject and addresses are sanitised (no newline characters).
Send a test message with a subject containing a line break and confirm it is removed or rejected.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The mailer strips or rejects line breaks in headers; test evidence in data/outbox.

plain: Applies to programs written in languages that manage memory by hand (C, C++). Node.js manages memory automatically, so this cannot happen here.

steps: Confirm the app has no native (compiled) modules.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No native modules are installed; the app runs on Node.js only.

plain: Numbers typed by users are checked to be within sensible ranges, so an absurdly large value cannot cause wrong results.

steps: Open each route schema and confirm number fields use z.number() with .min() and .max() or .int().
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Number fields have range limits in their schemas.

plain: Applies to languages where memory is freed by hand. Node.js frees memory automatically, so this cannot happen here.

steps: Confirm the app has no native modules.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Not applicable to a Node.js app.

plain: If the app read XML files, it would turn off features that let an XML file pull in other files from the server. The generated app does not parse XML.

steps: Search the code for an XML parser.
Confirm none is used, or that external entities are disabled.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No XML parsing library is installed.

plain: The app only reads data from outside as plain JSON and checks its shape. It never rebuilds program objects from untrusted data, which could run hidden code.

steps: Search for deserialisation libraries (node-serialize, unserialize) and confirm none is used.
Confirm incoming JSON is validated with zod before use.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Only JSON.parse plus schema validation is used for incoming data.

plain: There is a written list of what each input must look like (for example an email must be a valid email, a price must be a positive number). The app generates this list from its own checks in docs/validation.md.

manual.question: Does docs/validation.md exist and list the fields of your forms with their rules?
steps: Open docs/validation.md in the app folder.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The document lists every form and its field rules.

plain: The documentation describes checks between related fields (for example an end date must come after a start date).

steps: Read docs/validation.md and note any rules that combine two fields.
Compare with the business rules you expect (dates, quantities, totals).
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Cross-field rules relevant to your business are written down.

plain: Limits on how much a user or the whole app may do (for example 100 records per user, 20 uploads an hour) are written down.

manual.question: Do docs/validation.md and docs/SECURITY.md list the per-user quotas and rate limits?
steps: Open docs/validation.md and docs/SECURITY.md and look for the quota and rate-limit tables.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Documented limits per user and app-wide.

plain: Every piece of input is checked against what is expected (type, length, allowed values) before the app uses it.

steps: Confirm every route registered with defineRoute has a schema for params, query and body.
Submit a value of the wrong type (letters in a number field) and confirm a clear error.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: All routes have schemas; wrong input is rejected with a 400 response.

plain: Input checks happen on the server, not only in the browser. Browser checks are convenient but can be switched off by a visitor.

steps: Use a tool such as curl to send a form directly to the server with an invalid value, bypassing the browser.
Confirm the server rejects it.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A direct request with bad data receives a 400 validation error.

plain: Related fields are checked together so nonsense combinations are rejected (for example a booking that ends before it starts).

manual.question: When you enter an impossible combination, such as an end date before the start date, does the app refuse it?
steps: Try to save a record with an impossible combination of values.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The app shows an error and does not save the record.

plain: Multi-step processes (for example a checkout or a sign-up with confirmation) must be completed in order. A user cannot jump to the last step by typing its address.

manual.question: If you type the web address of a later step in a multi-step process without doing the earlier steps, are you sent back to the start?
steps: Start a multi-step flow, then paste the address of the final step directly into the browser.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The app redirects to the first step or shows an error.

plain: The limits written in the documentation (records per user, uploads per hour) are actually enforced by the app.

manual.question: When you exceed a documented limit, for example creating more records than allowed, does the app stop you?
steps: Pick a limit from docs/validation.md and try to exceed it.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The app refuses with a clear message once the limit is reached.

plain: When one action changes several things in the database, either all changes happen or none do. A half-finished change cannot leave data inconsistent.

steps: Search feature code for handlers that write more than one row.
Confirm they use withTransaction from src/db.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Multi-row writes are wrapped in withTransaction.

plain: Things that exist in limited numbers (appointment slots, seats, stock) cannot be double-booked by two people acting at the same moment.

steps: Identify limited resources in your app (slots, stock).
Confirm the database has a unique constraint or the code uses a transaction with a check before inserting.
Optionally send two booking requests at the same time and confirm only one succeeds.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A unique index or transactional check exists for each limited resource.

plain: The app slows down or blocks anyone who makes an unreasonable number of requests, so a script cannot flood it with junk, drain paid services or copy all the data.

manual.question: If you submit the same form many times very quickly, does the app eventually respond with a 'too many requests' message?
steps: Repeat a sign-up or password reset request more than the limit in docs/SECURITY.md.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A 'too many requests' response after the documented limit.

plain: Downloaded files and API responses are marked so browsers treat them as downloads or data, never as web pages. This stops an uploaded file from behaving like part of your site.

steps: Download an uploaded file and inspect the response headers.
Confirm Content-Disposition: attachment and Content-Security-Policy: sandbox are present.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Response headers for a file download include attachment and sandbox.

plain: Text that is meant to be shown as text is inserted into the page in a way that cannot run as code.

steps: Open public/js and confirm text is set with textContent, not innerHTML.
Confirm templates use <%= %> for data.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No innerHTML use with data; templates escape output.

plain: When the app runs over HTTPS, its cookies are marked Secure and named with the __Host- prefix, so they are never sent over an unencrypted connection.

steps: Run the app in TLS mode (selfsigned or behind a proxy).
Sign in and look at the Set-Cookie header in the browser developer tools.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The session cookie is named __Host-sid and has the Secure attribute.

plain: The session cookie is marked SameSite=Strict, which means other websites cannot make your browser send it. This blocks a common trick where another site performs actions as you.

steps: Sign in and inspect the Set-Cookie header in the browser developer tools.

plain: In HTTPS mode the session cookie name starts with __Host-, a browser rule that stops other sites or subdomains from overwriting it.

steps: Run the app in a TLS mode and inspect the session cookie name.

plain: The session cookie is marked HttpOnly so page scripts cannot read it, and the session value is only ever sent inside the cookie, never shown in a page or address.

steps: Sign in and inspect the Set-Cookie header.
Search page source for the session id value; it must not appear.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: HttpOnly is present and the session value appears nowhere in page content or URLs.

plain: When served over HTTPS, the app tells browsers to always use HTTPS for at least a year (HSTS), including for subdomains.

steps: With the app behind HTTPS, request any page and read the Strict-Transport-Security response header.
Confirm max-age is at least 31536000 and includeSubDomains is present.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The header value from a live HTTPS response.

plain: The app does not let other websites read its data from a browser (no cross-origin sharing). It never echoes back a requesting site's name.

steps: Send a request with an Origin header such as https://evil.example and inspect the response.
Confirm there is no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No CORS headers appear in responses.

plain: Every page carries a Content Security Policy, a browser rule that only allows scripts the app itself provided. Injected scripts are blocked even if some other defence fails.

steps: Request any page and read the Content-Security-Policy response header.
Confirm it contains object-src 'none', base-uri 'none' and a script-src with a nonce.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The header value from a live response.

plain: Every response tells browsers not to guess the type of content (X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff), which prevents a file from being mistaken for a script.

steps: Request a page, a stylesheet and an API endpoint and read the response headers.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff appears on every response.

plain: When a visitor clicks a link to another site, the browser is told not to reveal the full address of the page they came from, which may contain private details.

steps: Request any page and read the Referrer-Policy response header.

plain: Other websites cannot embed your app inside their own pages (frame-ancestors 'none'). This blocks 'clickjacking', where a hidden copy of your page tricks users into clicking.

steps: Read the Content-Security-Policy header of any response and look for frame-ancestors 'none'.

plain: Every form or action that changes data carries a secret token that other websites cannot know, so another site cannot submit actions as a signed-in user (CSRF protection).

steps: Sign in, open a form, remove the hidden _csrf field using the browser tools and submit.
Confirm the app rejects the request.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A submission without the token is refused with a 403 error.

plain: Applies to apps that rely on browser 'preflight' checks for protection. This app uses tokens instead, so this does not apply.

steps: Confirm the app has no CORS middleware and uses CSRF tokens.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No CORS configuration exists; CSRF tokens are enforced.

plain: Actions that change data only work with POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE requests, never with a plain link (GET). A plain link could be triggered by an image on another site.

steps: Read routes.manifest.json and confirm no GET route creates, changes or deletes data.
Try loading a delete or update address directly in the browser and confirm nothing changes.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: routes.manifest.json shows mutations only on non-GET methods.

plain: Separate applications should live on separate hostnames so browsers keep them apart. You only run one app, so this does not apply unless you host several on one name.

steps: If you host more than one app, confirm each has its own hostname.

plain: Applies to pages that receive messages from other browser windows (postMessage). The generated app does not use this feature.

steps: Search public/js for postMessage or a 'message' event listener.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: No postMessage listener exists, or it checks event.origin.

plain: The app uses only modern browser technology (plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript) and nothing obsolete like Flash or Java applets.

steps: Search views and public for <object>, <embed>, <applet> tags.

plain: The app will only send visitors on to addresses inside the app itself or on an approved list, so a crafted link cannot bounce people to a fake site.

steps: Search the code for res.redirect and confirm it uses safeRedirect.
Request a page with a redirect parameter such as ?next=https://evil.example and confirm you stay on the app.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: All redirects go through safeRedirect; an external target is ignored.

plain: Every response says what type of content it is and that it uses UTF-8 text, so browsers never have to guess.

steps: Request a page and an API endpoint and read the Content-Type header.

plain: When the app goes online, only pages for people should quietly switch from HTTP to HTTPS. API calls should fail instead, so a misconfigured program does not send data unencrypted without anyone noticing.

steps: Check the reverse proxy configuration: HTTP to HTTPS redirect for browser pages only; /api paths return an error over plain HTTP.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Proxy configuration showing the redirect rule excludes /api.

plain: Visitors cannot fake the headers that a proxy adds (such as their IP address). The app ignores X-Forwarded-For unless you have configured how many proxies sit in front of it.

steps: Read TRUST_PROXY_HOPS in .env; it must match the number of proxies in front of the app (0 when none).
Send a request with a made-up X-Forwarded-For header and confirm the logged IP is your real one.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: TRUST_PROXY_HOPS matches your setup and the spoofed header is ignored in logs.

plain: Every component in front of the app (proxy, load balancer) reads request boundaries the same way, so an attacker cannot smuggle a hidden second request inside a first one.

steps: Confirm the reverse proxy is a current version and uses HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 to the app with default strict parsing.
Confirm no custom settings relax Transfer-Encoding or Content-Length handling.

plain: Applies to GraphQL APIs, which can be overloaded with deeply nested queries. The generated app uses a plain JSON API, not GraphQL.

steps: Confirm no GraphQL library is installed.

plain: Applies to GraphQL's built-in 'introspection' feature, which reveals the whole API structure. The generated app does not use GraphQL.

steps: Confirm no GraphQL library is installed.

plain: Applies to live two-way connections (WebSockets). The generated app does not use them.

steps: Confirm no WebSocket library is installed.

plain: Applies to WebSocket connections, which must check where the connection comes from. The generated app does not use WebSockets.

steps: Confirm no WebSocket library is installed.

plain: Applies to WebSocket connections that need their own session tokens. The generated app does not use WebSockets.

steps: Confirm no WebSocket library is installed.

plain: Applies to handing an existing signed-in session over to a WebSocket connection. The generated app does not use WebSockets.

steps: Confirm no WebSocket library is installed.

plain: The documentation says which file types, extensions and sizes uploads may have, and what happens to a file that fails the checks.

manual.question: Does docs/uploads.md list the allowed file types, the size limit and what happens to rejected files?
steps: Open docs/uploads.md in the app folder.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The document lists types, extensions, size limits and rejection behaviour.

plain: Uploads larger than the configured limit are cut off during transfer, so a huge file cannot fill the disk or freeze the app.

manual.question: When you upload a file larger than the limit in docs/uploads.md, is it refused?
steps: Try uploading a file bigger than UPLOAD_MAX_BYTES (default 10 MB).
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The upload fails with a 'file too large' message.

plain: The app looks inside each uploaded file to confirm it really is the type its name claims (a .png that is really a program is refused).

manual.question: When you rename a text file to photo.png and upload it, is it refused?
steps: Rename a .txt file to .png and try to upload it.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The upload is rejected because the content does not match the type.

plain: Compressed files (zip) could expand to enormous sizes. The app refuses zip and similar archives entirely.

manual.question: When you try to upload a .zip file, is it refused?
steps: Try uploading a small .zip file.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The upload is rejected as a disallowed type.

plain: Uploaded files are stored outside the web folder under random names, so they can never be run as part of the app.

steps: Upload a file and locate it under DATA_DIR/uploads.
Confirm the stored name is a random id and that DATA_DIR is not under public/.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Stored file path is DATA_DIR/uploads/<uuid> and public/ contains no uploads.

plain: The app never uses a user-supplied file name to decide where a file is saved or read. It uses its own generated ids, so a name like ../../secret cannot reach other files.

steps: Search the code for path.join and fs calls and confirm the path never includes user input.
Upload a file named ../../test.png and confirm it is stored under a random id.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: File paths are built from generated ids only.

plain: When a file is downloaded, the app sets the file name itself (from its own records), not from anything in the request.

steps: Download a file and read the Content-Disposition header.
Confirm the filename comes from the stored record even if you add a filename parameter to the request.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Content-Disposition names the file from the database.

plain: File names in download headers are cleaned and encoded so a strange name cannot break the response or inject content.

steps: Upload a file with quotes, a semicolon and non-ASCII letters in its name.
Download it and confirm the Content-Disposition header is well formed (ASCII fallback plus filename*).
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A well-formed header for a tricky file name.

plain: Files from outside should be scanned for viruses. The generated app does not include a virus scanner; if you accept files from the public, add one on the server.

steps: Install a virus scanner (for example ClamAV) on the server.
Configure it to scan DATA_DIR/uploads regularly or on write.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Scanner installation and a recent scan log.

plain: There is a written description of how the app slows down and blocks password-guessing attacks (limits per account and per network address) and why a real user cannot be locked out permanently.

manual.question: Does docs/SECURITY.md describe the login limits and say that lockouts are temporary?
steps: Open docs/SECURITY.md and read the 'Login protection' section.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The section lists the limits and the temporary lock behaviour.

plain: There is a list of words that must not appear in passwords, such as your business name and the app name, because attackers try those first.

manual.question: Does docs/SECURITY.md list your business name and app name as banned password words?
steps: Open docs/SECURITY.md and look for the 'context words' list.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The list includes the app name and business name.

plain: If there were several ways to sign in, each would be documented with the same strength. This app has one sign-in method (password, plus an authenticator app for administrators), described in docs/SECURITY.md.

manual.question: Does docs/SECURITY.md describe the single sign-in method and the administrator two-step check?
steps: Open docs/SECURITY.md and read the 'Signing in' section.

plain: Passwords must be at least 12 characters long (the standard minimum is 8; longer is safer).

manual.question: When you try to set an 11-character password, is it refused?
steps: Open the change-password page and try a password of 11 characters.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The app shows a 'too short' message.

plain: Users can change their own password.

manual.question: Can you find and use a change-password page in your account settings?
steps: Sign in, open Account, change your password and sign in again with the new one.

manual.question: Does the change-password page ask for your current password?
steps: Open the change-password page and try changing it with a wrong current password.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The change is refused when the current password is wrong.

plain: New passwords are checked against a list of about 100,000 commonly used passwords and refused if they appear on it.

manual.question: When you try to set the password 'password1234', is it refused as too common?
steps: Try setting a well-known password such as password1234 or 123456789012.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The app refuses with a 'too common' message.

plain: Any characters are allowed in a password. There are no rules demanding capitals, numbers or symbols, because length matters more than mixing character types.

manual.question: Can you set a password made only of lowercase words, such as 'correct horse battery staple'?
steps: Try setting a long password with only lowercase letters and spaces.

plain: Password boxes hide what is typed.

manual.question: Are the characters hidden when you type in the password box?
steps: Open the sign-in page and type in the password field.

plain: Users can paste passwords and use password managers. Blocking paste only makes people choose weaker passwords.

manual.question: Can you paste a password into the sign-in page and the change-password page?
steps: Copy a password from a text file and paste it into the password box.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Paste works in all password fields.

plain: The app checks the password exactly as typed. It does not trim spaces or ignore capital letters.

manual.question: If you sign in with your password typed in different capitalisation, is it refused?
steps: Try signing in with the same password with one letter changed from lower to upper case.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: Sign-in fails with the altered password.

plain: Very long passwords (at least 64 characters) are accepted, so people can use long passphrases.

manual.question: Can you set a 70-character password?
steps: Set a password of 70 characters and sign in with it.

steps: Search the code for a password expiry or 'must change after N days' setting.
Confirm the only forced change is for the first-time administrator password.

plain: The banned context words (business name, app name, the user's own name and email) are actually refused inside new passwords.

manual.question: When you try a password that contains your app's name, is it refused?
steps: Try setting a password that includes the app name.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: The app refuses with a message about the app name.

steps: Decide whether to add a breach check (for example the Have I Been Pwned range API) in src/security/password.ts.
If added, test with a known-breached password.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A breach check is implemented and tested, or a written decision not to add one.

plain: Repeated wrong sign-in attempts are slowed down and temporarily blocked, as described in the documentation, so nobody can guess passwords by trying thousands of them.

manual.question: After several wrong passwords in a row, does the app make you wait?
steps: Enter a wrong password six times in a row for your own account.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: A 'please wait' or 'too many attempts' message.

plain: There are no built-in accounts with known passwords (like admin/admin). The first administrator gets a random one-time password that must be changed.

steps: Check that FIRST-LOGIN.txt no longer exists in the app folder.
Try signing in with admin/admin and confirm it fails.
manual.whatCountsAsEvidence: FIRST-LOGIN.txt is gone and default credentials do not work.

plain: Signing in should need more than a password. Administrators must use an authenticator app; other users can turn it on. Consider requiring it for everyone who sees sensitive data.
